title: Rye Well Depth and Drilling Cost Guide
meta_description: Rye wells have a 103 ft median depth, 7.5 gpm median yield, and typical finished costs of $9,600-$17,700.
h1: Rye, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
These records cover permitted wells within 5 miles of Rye in Pueblo County. They show a mostly domestic well area on the plains, with wells commonly completed in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers rather than the Denver Basin. For a buyer, the local pattern is fairly useful: the median well is 103 feet deep, the median reported yield is 7.5 gallons per minute, and the median static water level is 55 feet below ground.

Those figures are planning information, not a guarantee for a particular lot. Ground conditions, the exact location, casing and grout requirements, access, and the well’s permitted use still control the final result.

sections.heading: Rye wells are usually shallow, but the range is wide
sections.html:
Rye’s recorded wells have a median total depth of 103 feet. The middle half runs from 71 to 200 feet, meaning a driller bidding a normal residential well will usually be working within that range, not automatically planning for a deep hole. Still, the local record has a long tail: the 90th percentile is 360 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 1,405 feet.

Depth is split fairly evenly around the shallow range. 40% of wells are under 100 feet, while 46% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Another 12% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 2% exceed 600 feet. Alluvium and plains sedimentary rock help shape drilling conditions, but a nearby well is still the best first comparison.

sections.heading: Most Rye wells make usable household volumes
sections.html:
Among the wells that report a pump yield, the median is 7.5 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 5.0 and 13.0 gallons per minute. That is a workable range for ordinary household use when the well, pressure tank, storage, and plumbing are properly designed. It does not mean the well can produce that rate continuously without testing and confirming the well’s recovery.

The low-yield tail matters when comparing properties. 4% of reported wells produce under 1 gallon per minute, and 19% produce between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. Meanwhile, 56% are in the 5 to 15 gallon-per-minute range and 21% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Ask for the well yield test, not just a seller’s verbal estimate.

sections.heading: Rye water levels look broadly steady in the records
sections.html:
The median static water level is 55 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 30 to 150 feet. A shallow water level can reduce pumping lift, but it does not by itself prove that the well will produce enough water or that the water is suitable to drink. Static level, pumping level, recovery, and water quality are separate questions.

The decade comparison does not show a clear dropping trend in these records. The median measurement was 56 feet below ground in the 2010s and 52 feet in the 2020s. Only 61 wells report a static water level, so treat that comparison as a local indicator rather than a guarantee for an individual parcel. A current measurement is more useful when evaluating an existing well.

sections.heading: Rye permit history shows long-running local drilling
sections.html:
Rye has a long well-permit history, with 1,256 permitted wells in the mapped area and 884 recorded as constructed. Permits were issued across every decade listed in the records, including 23 in the 1950s, 216 in the 1990s, and 68 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most active drillers named in these records are Reeves, Mark, with 126 wells; Arkansas Valley Drilling (Moore, Todd A.), with 101; and Spradlin Drilling (Spradlin, Wayne), with 95. These names can help you research local history, but confirm current licensing, availability, scope, and references before selecting a contractor.

sections.heading: A median-depth Rye well pencils out at a defined range
sections.html:
For alluvium and plains sedimentary rock near Rye, the drilling-rate model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the local median depth of 103 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $3,600 to $5,700. That is the hole itself, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $9,600 to $17,700 at the median depth. A deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, longer trenching, or electrical work can move the bid outside that range. Get the driller to separate drilling, casing, grout, development, pump equipment, testing, and site restoration so competing bids are actually comparable.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic setbacks, and the build site
sections.html:
The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 historic mine features. It has 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That is not a property-specific safety clearance. Test an existing well for the contaminants relevant to the site and its history, and have a new well tested after construction before relying on it for drinking water.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible even where nearby records look favorable, especially around fractured bedrock. Confirm the permitted use: 93% of local wells are domestic or household wells, while stock, irrigation, and monitoring uses are also recorded. Before building, verify well access for a rig, septic separation and soil requirements, legal water use, and the location of the house, driveway, septic system, and utility trench.

sections.heading: Use nearby wells to price and investigate a Rye lot
sections.html:
When buying near Rye, start with the Colorado DWR permit and construction records for the parcel and immediate neighbors. Compare depth, aquifer description, yield test, static and pumping levels, well age, casing, and current equipment. Records from Colorado City may offer useful context at about 5 miles, while Beulah Valley, Gardner, Walsenburg, Pueblo West, and La Veta are farther away and may not match Rye’s ground conditions.

For a vacant lot, make well feasibility part of the purchase investigation rather than waiting until after closing. Confirm a driller can reach the site, identify a compliant well location, and budget both the drilling range and the complete pump-and-site system. Colorado DWR permitting still applies, and an exempt household-use well has a 35 gallon-per-minute pumping limit. Over-appropriated basins may also require an augmentation plan.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Rye, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within 5 miles of Rye is 103 feet. The middle half runs from 71 to 200 feet, but local conditions vary. Forty percent of wells are under 100 feet, while 12% are between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 1,405 feet, so nearby well records matter when estimating a new hole.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Rye, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35-$55 per foot. At Rye’s 103-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $3,600-$5,700. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $9,600-$17,700. Access, deeper drilling, casing, grout, and site conditions can change the contractor’s final bid.

faq.q: How much water do Rye wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 7.5 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 5.0-13.0 gallons per minute. Four percent of reported wells produce under 1 gallon per minute, while 19% produce 1-5 gallons per minute. Request the actual yield test and recovery information for the property instead of relying on the area median.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Rye?
faq.a: The well records do not establish drinking-water safety. Within about 10 miles, the mapped area includes 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 historic mine features, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test an existing or newly completed well for site-appropriate contaminants, and use treatment based on laboratory results rather than assumptions.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Rye, Colorado?
faq.a: The available records do not show a clear decline. Median static water level was 56 feet below ground in the 2010s and 52 feet in the 2020s. However, only 61 wells report a static water level, so this is limited evidence. A current static and pumping-level check is more relevant to a specific Rye property.
